opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and they're complementary to what the labs are doing rather than in competition with it.

The first is just the shape of the incentives. Inside a foundation model lab, interpretability is one priority among many, and it's ultimately in service of that lab's own models and its own release timelines. That's completely reasonable, and some of the best interpretability work in the world has come out of those teams. But it means the research naturally gets pointed at the questions that matter most for that particular model, at that particular moment. An independent company can be pointed at the problem itself, which is: how do we actually understand what's happening inside these networks, generally, across architectures and across providers?

The second is that most of the models that are going to matter in the world aren't going to be trained by three or four labs. There are open-weight models, fine-tuned models, domain-specific models in biology, materials science, finance, healthcare. The people deploying those systems need interpretability tools too, and they're not going to get them from a lab whose job is to ship its own frontier model. So there's a real gap between where interpretability research happens today and where models are actually being used.

Third, there's a trust dimension. If you're a regulator, or an enterprise, or just the public, and you want some assurance about what a model is doing internally, there's value in having that understanding come from a party that isn't also the one selling the model. It's similar to why we have independent auditors in finance. It doesn't mean the internal teams aren't doing good work, it just means a healthy ecosystem has more than one set of eyes on the problem.

And finally, I'd say there's a talent and focus argument. When interpretability is the entire company, the whole organization is oriented around turning research insights into tools that actually work at scale: things you can use to debug a model, edit its behavior, find where it's going wrong. That's a different kind of mission than doing interpretability as a research function inside a bigger effort. I think the field benefits from having both: the deep, model-specific work inside the labs and an independent group trying to make interpretability a general-purpose capability that anyone building with AI can use.

r001.rationale: The response describes an independent company working across architectures, providers, and open-weight and domain-specific models, giving it a broader view than a lab focused on its own models.

r002.rationale: The response says independent research can target understanding networks generally across architectures and providers, but it does not explain how synthesizing insights across different domains reveals more about their inner workings.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd start by saying the teams inside the labs are excellent, and some of the most important work in the field has come out of them. So the argument for an independent company isn't that they're doing it wrong. It's that there are a few things an independent company can do that a lab team structurally cannot, and I think the field needs both.

The first is cross-model work. If you sit inside one lab, you understand one family of models deeply, and that's incredibly valuable. But a lot of the interesting questions in interpretability are about what generalizes. Do the same features show up across architectures? Do the same circuits form regardless of training data? Are the failure modes universal or idiosyncratic? Those questions almost require you to be model-agnostic, to be able to open up a model from one lab on Monday and a model from a different lab on Tuesday and compare them honestly. An independent company can do that in a way that's very hard from inside a single organization.

The second is incentives. The lab teams are, understandably, oriented around the lab's own models and the lab's own roadmap. Interpretability work there has to compete for compute and attention with the next training run, and when there's tension between shipping and understanding, shipping tends to win. That's not a criticism, it's just what happens when the product is the model. An independent company gets to make interpretability the product. The whole organization is pointed at understanding, not at building something that then also needs to be understood.

The third thing, and this is the one I care about most, is who gets to use the tools. Right now, the deepest interpretability capabilities live inside a handful of organizations. If you're an enterprise deploying these systems, or a regulator trying to evaluate them, or an academic who wants to study them, you're mostly relying on what the labs choose to publish. An independent company can build this as infrastructure that other people actually get to use. I think of it a bit like auditing. You want the companies to have strong internal controls, but you also want someone external who can look at the books, and whose credibility comes partly from the fact that they don't have a stake in the answer.

And then there's a practical point about talent. Not everyone who wants to work on this problem wants to work inside a frontier lab, for all sorts of reasons. Having more places where serious interpretability research can happen just grows the field. The labs have been generous about publishing, and we build on that constantly. Ideally it goes the other way too, where things we figure out working across many models flow back and make everyone's internal teams better. That's the version of this that I think is healthy. Not competition, but a field that's bigger than any one lab.

r001.rationale: The response presents cross-model work as a distinctive benefit: an independent company can compare models from different labs and investigate what generalizes across architectures and training data.

r002.rationale: It describes comparing features, circuits, and failure modes across architectures and training data to identify what is shared or general, which communicates how cross-domain synthesis can deepen understanding of neural networks broadly.

astra-6.text:
I think teams inside the labs have some real advantages. They’re close to the models, they have access to the training process, and they can connect research directly to the systems they’re building. But there’s also value in having people outside those organizations asking independent questions about how the models work.

An independent company can work across models and across labs. That gives you a chance to distinguish between something that’s specific to one model and something more general. And you can focus on the needs of people deploying these systems, who may have very different questions from the people training them.

There’s also a trust component. If interpretability is going to help us assess whether a model is behaving the way we want, it’s useful for that assessment to come from more than just the organization that built it. I see those efforts as complementary: internal teams have depth and access, and independent teams can bring a broader perspective and another source of scrutiny.

r001.rationale: The response says an independent company can work across models and labs, distinguish model-specific findings from general ones, and bring a broader perspective.

r002.rationale: The response discusses comparing models and labs, but does not explain that synthesizing insights across different domains reveals more about neural networks’ inner workings generally.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the teams inside the labs have some real advantages. They have access to the models, the training process, and the people building them. But their work is also shaped by the priorities of that particular lab.

An independent company can focus on making interpretability useful across models and across organizations. If you’re a company deploying a model, you might want to understand why it behaves a certain way, whether you can trust it in a particular setting, or what changes when you switch models. Those questions don’t necessarily line up with a foundation model lab’s research roadmap.

There’s also value in having an independent perspective. The organization building a model shouldn’t be the only organization developing the tools to understand it. We can complement the work inside labs by turning research into tools that other people can use to investigate models and test claims for themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says an independent company can work across models and organizations, offering a perspective beyond any one lab’s priorities.

r002.rationale: It describes making tools usable across organizations, but does not say that synthesizing insights across domains reveals more about neural networks’ inner workings generally.
